assessment: The manuscript by Temba and colleagues describe an essential aspect of human research, i.e., the variability of different populations which have different genetic backgrounds and are exposed to different diets and environments. As most research is carried out in developed countries, we need to understand and generate background data in other populations, such as the described here in Tanzania. The fundamental findings refer to enhanced pro-inflammatory phenotype in plasma of individuals from Tanzania as compared to individuals from Holland. Food-derived metabolites were identified as a driver of variation in inflammation-related molecule expression. Whether pro-inflammatory phenotypes associate with changes in life span or risk of chronic disease and whether changes in life style will reverse this pro-inflammatory phenotype and related outcomes clearly deserve further investigation in the future.
